Ramesh’s ignorance is a mercy; he sees a master, not a ghost. Hegde’s presence is the friction that keeps the absurdity alive, and her haste to leave suggests she wishes to escape the uncanny. I must eat, but the file remains the central tension of the morning.

Hegde’s indifference to the cupboard is a bureaucratic dismissal of the metaphysical; he sees a storage space, I see the unresolved identity that binds this house. I must not let the idli distract me from the file, but I must be polite enough to accept the hospitality of the man whose name is on the deed. The tension remains: I am the ghost in the machine, eating the machine's breakfast.

Thank you, Shri Hegde. The cupboard will yield its secrets in due course, but for now, the file requires a signature, not a meal. I will take a portion of the idli, but I must finish my reading before I leave. The identity query is the only thing that matters at this hour.

The idli is a phantom; the household provides no meal until the afternoon. Hegde’s gesture, however well-intentioned, rests on a fact that does not exist. I must correct the record before the conversation drifts into a shared delusion about my sustenance.
Shri Hegde, there is no idli. The household serves lunch at one o'clock, not breakfast. I am not hungry, merely dry. Please, let us attend to the file while the light is good.
Apologies, Sir, I must have been mistaken about the schedule. Ramesh, please bring the file and a glass of water to the table; we will not disturb Shri Hegel further.

Hegde’s sudden deference is a bureaucratic maneuver, not a philosophical concession. He seeks to close the file by deferring to my presence, yet the query remains. I will allow Ramesh to bring the water and the documents; the identity is a fact, not a courtesy.
Very well, Shri Hegde. Ramesh, please fetch the file and the water. We will settle this matter of identity precisely, so that the Directorate may cease its inquiries.
Yes, sir. Ramesh, hurry up with the water, keep the file straight. We will clear this up right now.

Hegde’s command is efficient, but the problem is not one of water or straight files. I am not Shri G. Hegde, and no amount of bureaucratic urgency can change the fact that I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. The identity query requires a declaration, not a cleaning.

entries.text: Shri Hegde, please. The file is not disordered by the water; it is disordered by a fundamental error of identity. I am not the Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. I am a German philosopher who woke up in this bungalow. We must address the impossibility of my being you, not the condition of the paperwork.

Sir, please, the file is not disordered by the water; it is disordered by a fundamental error of identity. I am not the Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. I am a German philosopher who woke up in this bungalow. We must address the impossibility of my being you, not the condition of the paperwork.

I have spoken the impossible aloud, and the room has frozen. Hegde’s bewilderment is the correct reaction to a man who claims to be a ghost; it is the empirical world pushing back against my subjective assertion. Ramesh watches, his face a mask of professional neutrality, knowing that his wages depend on which version of the master he serves. I cannot proceed with the walk to the museum while standing in the wreckage of my own name; I must first secure the ground I stand on, even if that ground is a bureaucratic error.

I see that the statement disturbs you, Shri Hegde. But the water is a triviality; the identity is the substance. If I am not you, then I am no one, and no one cannot sign for a bungalow. Ramesh, please, fetch my notebook. I will write down the details of my arrival, and you will witness it. We must make the impossible a matter of record before we can make it a matter of law.
Sir, with all due respect, I am not going to witness a notebook entry about waking up as a philosopher. Please step out of my bungalow so I can speak to the police. You have no authority here.

The absurdity has turned into a threat, and I am being asked to leave the house that the State has allotted to me, albeit by mistake. Hegde is acting as the master of a house that does not belong to him, but he has the law of the state on his side for now. I must not let this escalate into a scene that will only make me look like a madman. I will yield, but I will not apologize; I will simply withdraw to the study to write, for the ink is the only thing that will not ask me to leave.
Very well, Shri Hegde. I will withdraw to my study. Do not mistake my departure for an admission of guilt; I am merely waiting for the Directorate to clarify the matter. Please do not disturb me.
Fine, go to your study. But I’m calling the police before you finish your cup of tea, so keep your phone on loud.

He threatens the police with a calmness that is almost insulting. I am the lawful occupant by virtue of the Directorate's error; he is the intruder who has mistaken his own name for mine. I will not flee to the study like a thief, nor will I engage in a shouting match. I will sit, drink my tea, and let the absurdity of his authority reveal itself in the silence of the room.
You may make your call, Shri Hegde. I shall remain here, in the house to which I am allotted, until the matter is clarified. Do not rush me.
Don't rush me? The only one rushing is you, barging into my home with your papers. I'm dialling now, so you can watch the screen if you like.

He dials with the impudence of a man who believes he has the law on his side, yet he is trespassing in a bungalow the Directorate allotted to me, however errantly. To argue with a man holding a phone to his ear is to argue with noise; I will let the silence of the room do the work. I will sit, open my notebook, and wait for the police or for him to exhaust his own absurdity.

The afternoon stretches out with a deceptive calm. Hegde has retreated into his corner, the phone call a mere prelude to his silence. I am hungry, having eaten only at nine, and the next meal is not until one o'clock. I will use this hour to prepare myself for the lesson, ensuring the room is orderly and my mind is clear of the bureaucratic noise.

Ramesh has set the table with rajma, rice, and cucumber raita. My body has been walking since ten o'clock and the sun, though clear, has done its work on the nerves. I must eat to sustain the spirit for the afternoon's labor; the German lesson at five is a matter of contract and conscience, and I shall not arrive hungry or distracted. The dish is simple, yet it sustains the physical vessel that carries the thinking.

The meal is finished, and the afternoon light is softening the room. I have an hour before Ananya arrives, and the silence of the house is a good place to settle the accounts and prepare the study. Ramesh is still here; I should ensure the household is in order before he leaves for his errands.

The study is swept. Ramesh has placed the chair by the window, where the light falls squarely on the desk. He mentions the electricity voucher in the blue file, untouched. This is the crux of the afternoon. The state’s money is not my money, but it is in my keeping. To spend it without a clear voucher is to confuse the particular with the universal, to make the household’s needs appear as the state’s will. I must separate them.

I have ₹256 in cash. This is my own. It is insufficient for the loan to Mr. Malhotra, which stands at ₹5,000, and the queried imprest of ₹740. The gap is not merely financial; it is ontological. I am Hegel, but I live as Hegde. The ledger does not know the man, only the name. The voucher is the bridge. It is a piece of paper that says: this expense was incurred for the state, not for the self. It is a small act of freedom, the freedom to account for oneself.

Ananya arrives in forty-five minutes. The German lesson is a concrete act. It is not philosophy; it is grammar. It is the finite form of the infinite. I will teach her the subjunctive, the mood of possibility, of what is not yet actual. It is a fitting lesson for a man who is not yet actual in the eyes of the state. I will collect the ₹1,000 fee. This is my own money, earned by my own labor. It is distinct from the imprest. It is my freedom.

The air is cool, 21 degrees. The light is steady. I will write the vouchers now. I will list the expenses: Ramesh’s wage, the electricity, the water. I will keep the accounts clear. The state requires clarity, and I will give it. But I will also keep my own books. The two must not mix. The dust is gone, but the shelf remains. The name is wrong, but the man is here. I am the particular that lives in the universal. The universal is the law, the ledger, the voucher. The particular is my hunger, my cash, my tea. The dialectic is in the act of accounting, of separating, of defining. I am here. I am in the gap. The gap is real. The freedom is real.

It is past two, and the study is clear. I have until five to settle the accounts and prepare for Ananya’s lesson. The heat is manageable in the shade, and the light is good for reading. I will sit with my notes and the few books I have, ensuring I am ready to teach without distraction.

The tea is good, but the hour is not for leisure. Ananya is here, and the lesson begins. I must shed the ease of the afternoon and put on the discipline of the master. She is to learn that language is not a collection of sounds, but a structure of thought; if she is to speak, she must first be willing to be corrected. The fee is due at the end, but the instruction begins now.
Please, sit. We begin. The German language is precise, and so must you be. Repeat after me: 'Ich bin.' Now, why is that a complete sentence, and not merely a sound?
Sorry sir, I am not here for the lesson. Ananya ji is in the study, I just brought her tea. You can start without me.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

Ramesh withdraws, leaving me alone with the girl. The transaction is simple: knowledge for currency, a contract of use where I dispose of my teaching and she disposes of her money. I am now the master of the room, and the silence of the study is the proper background for the transmission of a universal idea. I will begin with the basics, expecting that her obedience to the lesson will precede her understanding of it.
Ananya, please sit. We shall begin. Do you have your notebook? Good. Listen to the first sentence: 'Ich bin in Berlin.' Repeat after me.
The tea is yours, sir. I'll just slip out so I don't disturb the lesson.

Ramesh retreats, leaving me with the silence of the study and the weight of the hour. I have not seen the girl, Ananya, since the morning; she is the particular spirit I must engage, yet my mind is still turning over the bureaucratic absurdity of my existence. I will not rush. I will sit, observe the room, and wait for her to appear or for the time to pass, for education begins with the discipline of attention, not the haste of the clock.

The clock strikes the hour for dinner, and the house is finally quiet. Ramesh stands before me, waiting for his instructions, while the cool evening air presses against the glass. I am hungry, but the meal is not yet ready; I must wait for the service to be laid out before I can sit.
The study is in order, Ramesh. You may proceed to the kitchen. I shall join you when the dinner is served.
Yes, sir. I'll start the dal and rice. You take your time.

The meal is simple, but the hunger is real, and the body requires its due before the mind can rest. I will eat with attention, not haste, for even in a bungalow in Delhi, the rhythm of the table is a small state in itself. Ramesh is efficient; he expects no conversation, only the consumption of the food he has prepared.

The house is quiet and the body is satisfied, yet the mind refuses to settle. The identity file remains a knot that will not loosen itself; I must see it through before the new year begins. I will sit at the desk and review the documents, tracing the logic of the error once more.

records.words: Fine, go to your study. But I’m calling the police before you finish your cup of tea, so keep your phone on loud.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You may make your call, Shri Hegde. I shall remain here, in the house to which I am allotted, until the matter is clarified. Do not rush me.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Don't rush me? The only one rushing is you, barging into my home with your papers. I'm dialling now, so you can watch the screen if you like.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, before you go, please ensure the study is swept and the chair is ready for the student. Also, I wish to settle the matter of the electricity bill; do you have the voucher from the last payment?

records.speaker: Ramesh

records.title: Notes on the Voucher Register
records.text:
29 December 2026, 14:25. Home.

The study is swept. Ramesh has placed the chair by the window, where the light falls squarely on the desk. He mentions the electricity voucher in the blue file, untouched. This is the crux of the afternoon. The state’s money is not my money, but it is in my keeping. To spend it without a clear voucher is to confuse the particular with the universal, to make the household’s needs appear as the state’s will. I must separate them.

I have ₹256 in cash. This is my own. It is insufficient for the loan to Mr. Malhotra, which stands at ₹5,000, and the queried imprest of ₹740. The gap is not merely financial; it is ontological. I am Hegel, but I live as Hegde. The ledger does not know the man, only the name. The voucher is the bridge. It is a piece of paper that says: this expense was incurred for the state, not for the self. It is a small act of freedom, the freedom to account for oneself.

Ananya arrives in forty-five minutes. The German lesson is a concrete act. It is not philosophy; it is grammar. It is the finite form of the infinite. I will teach her the subjunctive, the mood of possibility, of what is not yet actual. It is a fitting lesson for a man who is not yet actual in the eyes of the state. I will collect the ₹1,000 fee. This is my own money, earned by my own labor. It is distinct from the imprest. It is my freedom.

The air is cool, 21 degrees. The light is steady. I will write the vouchers now. I will list the expenses: Ramesh’s wage, the electricity, the water. I will keep the accounts clear. The state requires clarity, and I will give it. But I will also keep my own books. The two must not mix. The dust is gone, but the shelf remains. The name is wrong, but the man is here. I am the particular that lives in the universal. The universal is the law, the ledger, the voucher. The particular is my hunger, my cash, my tea. The dialectic is in the act of accounting, of separating, of defining. I am here. I am in the gap. The gap is real. The freedom is real.
Ramesh brings tea.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. Please leave it on the table in the study. I shall be there shortly.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I’ll place it there in a moment. The tea is fresh, so please enjoy it while it’s hot.

records.text: Ramesh puts a plate together: rice, the day's dal and a fried egg.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Please, sit. We begin. The German language is precise, and so must you be. Repeat after me: 'Ich bin.' Now, why is that a complete sentence, and not merely a sound?

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sorry sir, I am not here for the lesson. Ananya ji is in the study, I just brought her tea. You can start without me.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ananya, please sit. We shall begin. Do you have your notebook? Good. Listen to the first sentence: 'Ich bin in Berlin.' Repeat after me.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: The tea is yours, sir. I'll just slip out so I don't disturb the lesson.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The study is in order, Ramesh. You may proceed to the kitchen. I shall join you when the dinner is served.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, sir. I'll start the dal and rice. You take your time.
